meta.subtitle: A topic-and-flow map of introductory electromagnetic field theory
meta.text: Sadiku, Elements of Electromagnetics, 6th ed. (section numbers are suggested reading, not required)

edgeKinds.requires: You need the source topic before the target topic makes sense.
edgeKinds.translates: Integral and differential forms of the same law, converted by a theorem.
edgeKinds.mirrors: The electrostatic / magnetostatic twin of a topic.

nodes.name: Vectors, dot & cross products
nodes.summary: Components, unit vectors, addition and subtraction, projections, and the two products. The cross product gives the direction of magnetic forces; the dot product gives flux and work.

nodes.name: Coordinate systems & constant surfaces
nodes.summary: Cartesian, cylindrical and spherical coordinates, how to transform between them, and the surfaces where one coordinate is held constant. Picking the coordinate system that matches the symmetry of a problem is most of the work in Gauss's and Ampère's laws.
nodes.equation: dl, dS, dv in each system

nodes.name: Line, surface & volume integrals
nodes.summary: Integrating a scalar or vector quantity along a path, over a surface, or through a volume. Every continuous charge or current distribution, every flux, and every circulation is one of these integrals.

nodes.name: Flux — "how much passes through"
nodes.summary: The surface integral of a vector field: how much of the field pokes through a surface. Flux is the physical meaning of the whole left column of Maxwell's equations. Read divergence as 'flux per unit volume'.

nodes.name: Circulation — "how much goes around"
nodes.summary: The closed line integral of a vector field: how much the field pushes you along a loop. Circulation is the physical meaning of the right column of Maxwell's equations. Read curl as 'circulation per unit area'.

nodes.name: Gradient
nodes.summary: The direction and rate of steepest increase of a scalar field. Gradient never appears in Maxwell's equations directly; it is how you climb back from a potential to a field.

nodes.name: Divergence
nodes.summary: Net outward flux per unit volume at a point. Positive where field lines start, negative where they end, zero where they just pass through.

nodes.name: Curl
nodes.summary: Circulation per unit area at a point, as a vector along the axis of rotation. A field with zero curl everywhere is conservative and has a scalar potential.

nodes.name: Divergence theorem
nodes.summary: Total flux out of a closed surface equals the volume integral of the divergence inside it. This is the translator between the integral and differential forms of Gauss's law and of ∇·B = 0.

nodes.name: Stokes' theorem
nodes.summary: Circulation around a closed loop equals the flux of the curl through any surface bounded by the loop. This is the translator between the integral and differential forms of Ampère's law and of ∇×E = 0.

nodes.name: Charge distributions
nodes.summary: Discrete point charges, and line, surface and volume charge densities. Charge is the source of the electric field; a continuous distribution is handled by integrating over infinitesimal point charges.
nodes.equation: Q = ∫ ρ_L dl = ∫ ρ_S dS = ∫ ρ_v dv

nodes.name: Coulomb's law
nodes.summary: The force between two point charges, from Coulomb's torsion-balance experiment. Dividing out the test charge defines the electric field. The explicit solution to the 'divergence' half of electrostatics.

resources.label: oPhysics · Coulomb forces on three charges

nodes.name: The electric field E
nodes.summary: Force per unit charge on a test charge. Fields of discrete charges add as vectors; fields of continuous distributions are integrals of Coulomb's law. Field lines start on positive charge and end on negative charge.

nodes.name: The electric dipole
nodes.summary: Two equal and opposite charges a small distance apart. Its field falls off as 1/r³, and it is the building block for polarization in dielectrics.

nodes.name: Gauss's law (integral)
nodes.summary: The total electric flux out of any closed surface equals the enclosed charge over ε₀. Maxwell's first equation in the form you can compute with: pick a surface that matches the symmetry and the integral collapses.

nodes.name: Gauss's law (differential)
nodes.summary: The divergence of E at a point equals the charge density there over ε₀. Same law as the integral form, translated by the divergence theorem. This is the form that leads to Poisson's equation.

nodes.name: Applying Gauss: symmetry & composite structures
nodes.summary: Spheres, infinite lines and planes, coaxial cables, nested shells. The recipe: identify the symmetry, choose the matching Gaussian surface, pull |E| out of the integral, solve region by region.

nodes.name: E is conservative:  ∮ E·dl = 0
nodes.summary: The work done moving a charge around any closed loop in a static electric field is zero, so the work between two points is path-independent. This is what makes a scalar potential possible.

nodes.name: ∇×E = 0
nodes.summary: The static electric field has no curl anywhere. Translated from the integral form by Stokes' theorem. This cell of Maxwell's equations is where Faraday's law appears once fields vary in time.

nodes.name: Electric potential V
nodes.summary: Work per unit charge to bring a test charge in from a reference point. A scalar, so it adds as a number rather than a vector. E is the negative gradient of V; V is the negative line integral of E.

resources.label: oPhysics · Charged particle in an electric field

nodes.name: Energy in charge distributions & in the field
nodes.summary: The work to assemble a set of charges, which can be rewritten as an energy density stored in the field itself. The field-energy form is what you use for capacitors.
nodes.equation: W = ½ ∫ ρ_v V dv = ½ ∫ ε₀ E² dv

nodes.name: Poisson's & Laplace's equations
nodes.summary: Substitute E = −∇V into ∇·E = ρ/ε₀ and you get one scalar equation for V. With no charge in the region it becomes Laplace's equation. Solving these with boundary conditions is the general method of electrostatics.

nodes.name: Numerical methods: mesh grids & iterative solvers
nodes.summary: Discretize space onto a grid, replace derivatives with differences, and iterate until the potential stops changing. Accuracy versus runtime is the trade-off; this is what field simulation software does under the hood.

nodes.name: Conductors: induced charge, current, resistance
nodes.summary: Inside a perfect conductor in equilibrium E is zero and the surface is an equipotential; charge rearranges on the surface to make it so. With a steady current, Ohm's law in field form gives the resistance of a structure.
nodes.equation: J = σE,  R = V/I = ∫ dl / (σ S)

nodes.name: Polarization P & bound charge
nodes.summary: An applied field stretches or aligns the molecular dipoles in a dielectric. The net effect is equivalent to bound surface and volume charge, which partially cancels the applied field.
nodes.equation: P = dipole moment / volume,  ρ_b = −∇·P,  ρ_sb = P·â_n

nodes.name: Displacement field D & permittivity
nodes.summary: Define D so that its flux depends only on the free charge you control, hiding the bound charge. In a linear dielectric D is just ε times E. Gauss's law in a dielectric is Gauss's law with D and free charge.
nodes.equation: D = ε₀E + P = εE,  ∮ D·dS = Q_free

nodes.name: Boundary conditions for E and D
nodes.summary: At an interface, tangential E is continuous and the jump in normal D equals the surface charge. Both follow directly from the integral forms: a tiny loop for the tangential condition, a tiny pillbox for the normal one.

nodes.name: Capacitance, stored energy, fringe fields
nodes.summary: Charge stored per volt between two conductors, a property of the geometry and the dielectric only. Compute it from Q/V or from the stored energy. Real capacitors have fringe fields at the edges that the ideal formulas ignore.

nodes.name: Current distributions
nodes.summary: Line currents, surface current density K and volume current density J. Moving charge is the source of the magnetic field, in the same way static charge is the source of the electric field.

nodes.name: Biot–Savart law
nodes.summary: The magnetic field of a current element, from Ampère's and Biot and Savart's experiments. It plays the role Coulomb's law plays in electrostatics: the explicit solution you integrate over the source.

nodes.name: The magnetic field B
nodes.summary: Fields of straight wires, loops and solenoids come from integrating Biot–Savart. Field lines of B always close on themselves; they never start or end anywhere.

nodes.name: Lorentz force
nodes.summary: The force on a moving charge in electric and magnetic fields. The only equation in this course containing both E and B, and so the one place the two halves of the map touch directly.

resources.label: oPhysics · Charged particle in a magnetic field

nodes.name: Forces between currents; torque & moment
nodes.summary: Sum the Lorentz force over the charges in a wire and you get the force on a current element in a field, then the force between two wires. A current loop in a field feels a torque, which defines its magnetic dipole moment.
nodes.equation: dF = I dl × B,  T = m × B,  m = I S â_n

nodes.name: Ampère's law (integral)
nodes.summary: The circulation of B around any closed loop equals μ₀ times the current threading the loop. The magnetostatic counterpart of Gauss's law: with the right symmetry the integral collapses and B falls out.

nodes.name: ∇×B = μ₀J
nodes.summary: The curl of B at a point is μ₀ times the current density there. Translated from the integral form by Stokes' theorem. In time-varying fields a displacement-current term joins J here.

nodes.name: Applying Ampère: symmetry & composite structures
nodes.summary: Infinite wires, coaxial cables, solenoids, toroids, current sheets. Same recipe as Gauss: find the symmetry, pick the Amperian loop that follows it, pull |B| out, solve region by region.

nodes.name: ∮ B·dS = 0
nodes.summary: The net magnetic flux out of any closed surface is zero: there are no magnetic charges for field lines to start or end on. Flux through an open surface is still meaningful and is what inductance is built on.

nodes.name: ∇·B = 0
nodes.summary: B has no divergence anywhere, in statics or otherwise. Translated from the integral form by the divergence theorem. Because of this, B can always be written as the curl of a vector potential.

nodes.name: Magnetic dipole, magnetization M & bound currents
nodes.summary: A small current loop is a magnetic dipole; a material full of aligned dipoles has a magnetization M. The net effect is equivalent to bound surface and volume currents, the magnetic twin of bound charge.
nodes.equation: M = dipole moment / volume,  J_b = ∇×M,  K_b = M × â_n

nodes.name: Auxiliary field H & permeability
nodes.summary: Define H so that its circulation depends only on the free current you control, hiding the bound currents. In a linear material B is just μ times H. Ampère's law in a material is Ampère's law with H and free current.
nodes.equation: H = B/μ₀ − M,  B = μH,  ∮ H·dl = I_free

nodes.name: Dia-, para- & ferromagnetism
nodes.summary: Diamagnets weakly oppose an applied field, paramagnets weakly follow it, and ferromagnets have domains that align strongly and stay aligned: saturation, hysteresis, and permanent magnets.

nodes.name: Boundary conditions for B and H
nodes.summary: At an interface, normal B is continuous and the jump in tangential H equals the surface current. Pillbox and loop arguments again, now applied to ∮B·dS = 0 and Ampère's law.

nodes.name: Flux linkage, self & mutual inductance
nodes.summary: Flux linked per ampere of current, a property of geometry and material only. Compute it from flux linkage or from stored energy. Real inductors have resistance, parasitic capacitance and leakage flux that the ideal formulas ignore.

nodes.name: Energy in the magnetic field & in an inductor
nodes.summary: The work to establish a current against its own induced field, rewritten as an energy density stored in the field. The second route to inductance.

nodes.name: Magnetic vector potential A
nodes.summary: Because ∇·B = 0, B can be written as the curl of some vector field A. It is the magnetic twin of the scalar potential V, and it is the quantity that becomes central once fields vary in time.

nodes.name: Time-varying fields
nodes.summary: The two 'empty' cells of the static Maxwell equations are where the action is once things move. A changing B puts a term into ∇×E = 0 (Faraday's law); a changing E puts a term into ∇×B = μ₀J (displacement current). That coupling is what makes waves, and it is the next course.

nodes.name: Antennas & RF
nodes.summary: Everything about radiating structures is Ampère's law, boundary conditions and material properties with time dependence added. Antenna design is where this course's symmetry arguments and material models get used for real.

nodes.name: Full EM solvers
nodes.summary: The iterative Laplace solver you build on a grid is the smallest version of what finite-difference and finite-element field solvers do. Meep is a free, serious one.

nodes.name: Circuits
nodes.summary: C and L are the two field quantities that survive into circuit theory as lumped elements. Circuit simulators let you see what the stored-energy formulas do in time.
nodes.equation: i = C dv/dt,  v = L di/dt

nodes.name: Fourier & signals
nodes.summary: Separable solutions of Laplace's equation are the first place Fourier series show up in field theory. From there the same mathematics runs all of signal processing and modern radio.
